segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You might have noticed that we're not using the word for "I". "Quiero" by itself means "I want".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: There is a word for "I". The word for "I" is "yo". Y-o, "yo".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And you only use it if you want to be emphatic. So if you want to say *I* want, and show that emphasis, how would you do it?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The same order as English: "I don't want".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Yo no quiero. I don't want. Good. "I don't want to cancel"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Yo no quiero cancelar. How would you say "celebration"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What would it mean if I say: "Quiero ilustrar. Quiero ilustrar"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. I want to illustrate. This is an interesting word as well, actually. The "luz" inside of "ilustrar" means "light". And the word "luz", l-u-z, so actually the z would be pronounced "th" in most of Spain, "luz", but in the rest of the Spanish-speaking world, "luz", means light. So you can use that word as well.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "I want to find out"? Now in Spanish, you would say something like "I want to inform myself", "I want to inform myself".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Very good. Quiero informarme. So how was "information"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was "you" in the sense of "I love you", "I want you"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Te. And this is informal "you", this is used informally.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say then "I don't want to oblige you"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you might think, "Oh, I don't know this." It's very important, sentences that we think we don't know, to take them block by block. And in this way, we will realize we can say so much in Spanish that we would have assumed that we don't know how to say.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So the first bit is "I don't want".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No quiero. "To oblige"? So we look to see if we have "obligation" in English. We have it, right? It's a word, it's legal. So how is that?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Obligar. Ah, so we don't want to jump from "oblige" to sticking -ar on it, you know? We want to take that long route: obligation, obligación, obligar. And then we find the word in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So: "I don't want", no quiero, "to oblige you"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No quiero obligarte. I don't want to oblige you. I don't want to make you do it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So in English, we would say "make you", maybe. Maybe "oblige" sounds a little bit too formal, but in Spanish, it's everyday language.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "I don't want to provoke you. I don't want to provoke you"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The word for "it" in Spanish is "lo".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, how would you say "I want to cancel it"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Quiero cancelarlo. How would you say "I want to regulate it"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I want to talk about this "r". An initial "r", like in "regular", in most Spanish dialects, it's a rolling "r". You get this flick of the tongue: regular, real—we saw this as well in "real", real. Now, if you can't make that sound, I don't want you to worry about it yet.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It's something that, you know, I couldn't pronounce it, actually. I couldn't pronounce it for a long time, and it was really frustrating, and I was trying to pronounce it. And when you're trying to pronounce it, your mouth gets tense. And actually, you need a very relaxed mouth to pronounce this "r" because you're kind of lifting your tongue up a little bit and letting the air flap it. Now, that's a muscle. If it's tense, the air can't flap it. So I tried a very long time, I got very frustrated, and I gave up. And then I was practicing Spanish in Peru. One day I started speaking about rice, which is "arroz", and the "r" came out all by itself, and I was so excited, and I was jumping up and down saying, "Arroz! Arroz! Arroz!" And then I heard, "The gringo is hungry."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But, my advice if you can't pronounce this sound is just to let it come. The more you hear, just because you want to pronounce it, it's going to come.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So an initial "r" or two r's together inside the word is going to pronounce this double r.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So the word for "but" in Spanish is "pero".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: P-e-r-o. And the word for "dog" is "perro". P-e-r-r-o.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So that's the difference. You have normal "r", pero—

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: —and it's a bit different to English because it's still kind of more pronounced, you know? You're still using your tongue more there: pero. And then perro, you keep that in the same position that you are using to make that Spanish "r", which is kind of a little bit more pronounced than the "r" English sound, but you pass a little bit of air over it and you let that flick it: perro.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, like I said, I don't want you to worry about if you can't pronounce this. There are even native Spanish speakers that can't pronounce this, so it's really something I don't want to inhibit anybody.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How do you think is "salvation" in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Salvación. So how do you think would be "to save"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: This word that we used for "it", "lo", can also mean "him".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say "I want to save him"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Quiero salvarlo. I want to save him.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now if you turn that into a verb, you actually get "to situate", to place, to put somewhere. So how would that be?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So take it syllable by syllable. This is very important so it doesn't become like a salad, you know? You want to take it syllable by syllable.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we want, we must take it—sometimes you don't need to take it slowly, but we want to get in the habit of taking it slowly, dividing up syllable by syllable. We want to install the correct process slowly. We don't want to jump from "participate" to "participar" because maybe we end up putting some extra sound, "participatar" or something like this, and we don't want to do this. We want to take the long route.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So for example, if you want to work out how to say "to create" in Spanish, you want to go through the long way. You want to go through "creation"—

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah, and that's it. That's the verb in Spanish: crear, to create.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah, that's it: experimentar. And this also means "to experience". To experiment and to experience, which is a little bit of wisdom that I really like there from Spanish, because your experience is like an experiment. If you think that your relationship with experience is scientific, you look what happens and you learn from it, or at least you should. So in Spanish, there is a suggestion of that in the fact that these words are the same: "to experience" and "to experiment" is the same verb, experimentar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The nouns are different. Experience is "experiencia"; experiment is "experimento". But the verb, the act, is the same verb: experimentar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Actually, this gives us another nice rule: experience, experiencia. If we have a word that ends in -ence or -ance, we can change -ence to -encia and -ance to -ancia, and we will get the word in Spanish.
